title: Humour and teasing
job: Banter, irony, and when not to
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: parihāsaḥ is a joke and a joke is something you MAKE: parihāsam karoti. kevalam is 'only, merely', and the two together are the whole frame — aham kevalam parihāsam kṛtavān, 'I was only joking'.

The retraction is the half worth learning. kṣamyatām (L2-M1) in front of the frame takes the joke back whole: kṣamyatām, aham parihāsam kṛtavān. The cost of a joke that misses in a second language is entirely in whether you can withdraw it.
hasati is 'laughs'. It is the RESPONSE and never the joke, so a sentence about humour usually needs both verbs: one person makes the parihāsaḥ and another laughs, or does not.

English teases in the second person and close up — 'you are always late'. This course addresses a listener as bhavān or bhavatī with a THIRD-person verb, which is a built-in polite distance, and the intimate second person is not on this ladder at all. The second-person jab is not written here, and no sentence below pretends to be one.
So the tease that works here is the one aimed at yourself, because it needs no second person: mama saṃskṛtam śrutvā aham eva hasāmi — 'hearing my own Sanskrit, I am the one who laughs'.

The pun — śleṣa — is the wit Sanskrit is famous for, and this course writes none. It works by one word carrying two readings, and four levels have deliberately chosen ONE reading for every word that could carry two: phalam is fruit and not a result, satyam is 'that's right' and not 'truth', yāvat and tāvat are time and not extent, yat introduces a clause and does not mean 'because', vā is 'or' and not a question tag, api is 'also' and not a question marker. The second readings are named here and written nowhere.

The wit this register carries most easily is a well-turned saying quoted for pleasure rather than instruction. L5-M1's subhāṣitāni are the material, and a line landed at the right moment is funnier here than any joke you could build.

English deadpan works because nothing marks it. An unmarked joke inside this polite frame is simply a rude sentence, so a joke here is the MARKED case: it is announced with kevalam parihāsaḥ or withdrawn with kṣamyatām, and often both.

When not to, first answer: the classical register belongs to teachers, ceremonies and texts, so a joke made in it reads as mock-pompous rather than funny. Keep humour in the everyday register this course speaks.

When not to, second answer: a tease aimed at a bhavān by someone the listener does not know reads as sarcasm rather than warmth, because the politeness of the frame and the content of the joke disagree. Say the retraction before you are asked for it.

words.note: L1-M1's 'I'. The participle at the end agrees with it, so the speaker's gender decides the last word of the sentence.
Only — and it is the word doing the apologising. Without it the sentence just reports that a joke was made; with it, the joke is being cut down to size.
A joke. The plain shape is parihāsaḥ and this is the object shape; the cue is written for the word rather than for the case, because the module uses both.
L1-M4's participial past of karoti, agreeing with the speaker. A woman saying this says kṛtavatī and nothing else changes.

sentences.trap: There is no verb for 'joke' in Sanskrit. A joke is a noun and you MAKE it, so the sentence needs karoti and its past, not a verb of its own.
sentences.sound: a-HAM KE-va-lam pa-ri-HAA-sam KRI-ta-vaan. The ṛ of kṛtavān is a vowel in its own right, said like the ri of 'rich' with the tongue curled. Said at speed all three m's soften to a hum: ahaṃ kevalaṃ parihāsaṃ kṛtavān. The page keeps every m.

variations.changed: a woman says it, so the participle forks and nothing else in the sentence moves
the frame turned outward to defend somebody else, which is the other half of what it is for
negated, and kevalam goes with the negation — 'not joking' is a denial, 'only joking' is a retreat, and they are different moves

mistake.why: parihāsaḥ is the shape a joke takes as the SUBJECT. Here the joke is what was made, so it takes the object shape parihāsam — the same -aḥ against -am the course has drawn since L1-M1.

sentences.usage: The single most useful sentence in this module, and the one to learn first. It is said immediately, before the listener has decided how to take what you said.
sentences.mnemonic: A joke is made, not spoken.

words.note: L2-M1's apology. It names nobody — literally 'let it be forgiven' — which is exactly why it can stand in front of any admission.
L1-M1's 'I'. The apology has no subject of its own, so the sentence's subject arrives with the second clause.
The joke, as the object of the making. Here it is being owned up to rather than explained away.
The participial past again, agreeing with the speaker. The retraction is in the past because the joke has already landed.

sentences.trap: kevalam is not in this sentence and its absence is the point. 'Sorry, I was joking' admits the joke; 'I was ONLY joking' argues about it, and after an apology that argument undoes the apology.
sentences.sound: ksham-ya-TAAM, a-HAM pa-ri-HAA-sam KRI-ta-vaan. kṣ is a single cluster, k and ṣ said together with the tongue curled back for the ṣ. Said at speed kṣamyatām aham runs straight on as kṣamyatāmahaṃ, the m keeping its m before the vowel.

variations.changed: apologising on somebody else's behalf, so the subject and the participle fork together

variations.display: kṣamyatām, aham parihāsam kṛtavān, idam kevalam parihāsaḥ.
variations.script: क्षम्यताम्, अहम् परिहासम् कृतवान्, इदम् केवलम् परिहासः।
variations.cue: Sorry — I was joking; it was only a joke.
variations.changed: a third clause spells out what the first two implied, which is what a speaker does when the apology has not landed
the apology moves to the end, where it repairs rather than warns; in front it prepares the listener, behind it patches them up

mistake.why: mama is 'my' and cannot be the subject of a participle. The participial past takes a nominative subject that it agrees with, so it must be aham here — the mistake reads as 'my joke made' with nobody doing anything.

sentences.usage: The clean retraction, and the module's core move. It is one word longer than the joke it withdraws, which is about the right ratio.
sentences.mnemonic: Apologise first, explain second, argue never.

words.note: L1-M1's 'this', pointing at what was just said. It does the job an English 'that' would do here, because the thing is close in time.
Only. It stands in front of the word it shrinks, which is the opposite of L5-M1's eva — eva lifts what precedes it, kevalam limits what follows.
The plain shape of the joke, because here it is the predicate and not the object. A verbless sentence needs it in exactly this shape.

sentences.trap: No verb, and none is missing: idam parihāsaḥ is 'this is a joke' with the 'is' left for the listener, the same shape as L1-M1's aham chātraḥ.
sentences.sound: i-DAM KE-va-lam pa-ri-HAA-sah. The final -ḥ of parihāsaḥ is a light echo of the a in front of it: 'pa-ri-haa-sa-ha'. Said at speed the first two words are idaṃ kevalaṃ, both m's softening to a hum.

variations.changed: L1-M2's kim turns the statement into the question a listener asks when they cannot tell — which is the question this whole module exists to prevent
L4-M8's āsīt puts it in the past, which is where a retraction usually has to reach
negated, and it is the sentence that ends the fun — worth knowing precisely so that it is not said by accident

mistake.why: The object shape has been used for a predicate. Nothing here is being done to the joke — the joke is what this IS — so it takes the plain shape parihāsaḥ, as any word standing after a silent 'is' does.

sentences.usage: Said about something already on the table: a remark, a message, a face somebody pulled. It is the label, where S01 is the confession.
sentences.mnemonic: kevalam looks forward, eva looks back.

words.note: L1-M2's question marker, standing first and asking nothing by itself. It turns the whole sentence into a yes/no question.
The course's 'you' since L1-M2, taking a THIRD-person verb. To a woman it is bhavatī, and the verb does not move.
The joke as the object again. Asking about somebody else's joke is as close to a tease as this register goes.
L1-M4's 'makes', third person because bhavān is third person. This is the present, where S01's kṛtavān was the past.

sentences.trap: The verb is third person even though you are talking TO someone. That is the whole register: bhavān is grammatically 'his honour', so the sentence is built as if about a third party and aimed at the person in front of you.
sentences.sound: KIM bha-VAAN pa-ri-HAA-sam KA-ro-ti. bh is a b with a real puff of breath and English has nothing like it. Said at speed kim bhavān is kiṃ bhavān, the m becoming a hum before the bh, and parihāsam karoti is parihāsaṃ karoti.

variations.changed: the listener is a woman, so the pronoun forks and the third-person verb stays exactly as it was
kim removed, so the question becomes a flat statement — and in this polite frame that reads as an accusation rather than a tease
asked about a third party instead of the listener, which is the safe version and the one to reach for with strangers

mistake.why: The joke is again in the subject shape where the sentence needs the object shape. bhavān is already the subject, and a Sanskrit sentence does not take two.

sentences.usage: Asking rather than assuming, which in this register is the polite move. Said flat it is a real question; the statement version of it is not a tease and should be avoided with anyone you do not know.
sentences.mnemonic: bhavān, and the verb still says 'he'.

sentences.display: aham kevalam parihāsam kṛtavān iti saḥ uktavān.
sentences.script: अहम् केवलम् परिहासम् कृतवान् इति सः उक्तवान्।
sentences.literal: I only joke made (quote-close) he said

words.note: The 'I' of the QUOTED speaker, not of the person reporting. Sanskrit quotes the words as they were said and does not shift the pronoun the way English does.
Only, inside the quotation. The frame is reported whole because the frame is what was actually said.
The joke, still the object of the quoted making.
Agreeing with the quoted aham — so this participle tells you the gender of the person who SPOKE, not of the person reporting it.
L3-M5's quote-closer, doing here what it did for a subhāṣita in L5-M1: it shuts the quotation and nothing opens it.
The reporter, arriving after the quotation. This is the course's fixed order: quoted line, iti, then who said it.
L3-M5's 'said', agreeing with saḥ. There are two participles in this sentence and they agree with two different people.

sentences.trap: Two participles, two subjects. kṛtavān belongs to the quoted aham and uktavān to saḥ, so a woman reporting a man's retraction writes kṛtavān and uktavatī.
sentences.sound: a-HAM KE-va-lam pa-ri-HAA-sam KRI-ta-vaan I-ti SAH UK-ta-vaan. Said at speed kṛtavān iti joins straight on as kṛtavāniti. There is a small pause before saḥ, which is where the quotation ends for a listener.

variations.display: aham kevalam parihāsam kṛtavatī iti sā uktavatī.
variations.script: अहम् केवलम् परिहासम् कृतवती इति सा उक्तवती।
variations.changed: both speakers are women, so both participles fork — and they fork independently, which is the point

variations.display: aham kevalam parihāsam kṛtavān iti saḥ na uktavān.
variations.script: अहम् केवलम् परिहासम् कृतवान् इति सः न उक्तवान्।
variations.cue: He did not say, 'I was only joking.'
variations.changed: the FRAME is negated and the quotation is untouched — na stands before uktavān and never inside the quoted words

variations.display: aham kevalam parihāsam kṛtavān iti saḥ vadati.
variations.script: अहम् केवलम् परिहासम् कृतवान् इति सः वदति।
variations.changed: the reporting verb moves to the present with L2-M7's vadati, while the quoted past stays where it was

mistake.display: aham kevalam parihāsam kṛtavān saḥ uktavān.
mistake.why: iti has been dropped, so nothing marks where the quotation ends. Without it a listener hears two subjects colliding — aham and saḥ — and no way to tell which words belonged to whom.

sentences.usage: How the retraction gets passed on. It is also the sentence that shows the register's real problem: reported at a distance, an apology reads as a fact, and a listener has to be told it was meant warmly.

sentences.display: saḥ parihāsam karoti, sā ca hasati.
sentences.script: सः परिहासम् करोति, सा च हसति।
sentences.cue: He makes a joke and she laughs.
sentences.literal: he joke makes, she and laughs

words.note: L1-M5's 'he', the one making the joke. The two clauses have different subjects, which is why both are written out.
The joke as the object of karoti, the pairing the whole module is built on.
L1-M4's 'makes'. Present, because this is what happens rather than what happened.
L1-M5's 'she', the second clause's subject. The two clauses are about two different people, which is why both subjects are written out.
L1-M10's 'and'. It stands AFTER the first word of what it joins, not between the two clauses the way English 'and' does.
Laughs. One row, three shapes: hasati for one person, hasanti for more than one, hasāmi for me. The cue is written for the word, not for the person.

sentences.trap: ca goes second, not first. English 'and she laughs' starts with the joiner; Sanskrit writes sā ca hasati, with ca tucked in behind the word it hooks on to.
sentences.sound: SAH pa-ri-HAA-sam KA-ro-ti, SAA CHA HA-sa-ti. c is the ch of 'church' — never the k of 'cat' and never an s. Said at speed parihāsam karoti is parihāsaṃ karoti, the m softening to a hum before the k.

variations.display: saḥ parihāsam karoti, aham ca hasāmi.
variations.script: सः परिहासम् करोति, अहम् च हसामि।
variations.cue: He makes a joke and I laugh.
variations.changed: the laugher becomes the speaker, so the verb takes its -āmi ending — the same row, a different person

variations.display: saḥ parihāsam karoti, kintu sā na hasati.
variations.script: सः परिहासम् करोति, किन्तु सा न हसति।
variations.cue: He makes a joke, but she does not laugh.
variations.changed: L1-M10's kintu replaces ca and the second clause is negated — the honest version, and the one that needs a retraction next

variations.display: saḥ parihāsam kṛtavān, sā ca hasati.
variations.script: सः परिहासम् कृतवान्, सा च हसति।
variations.cue: He made a joke and she is laughing.
variations.changed: the first clause moves to the participial past while the second stays in the present, which is what a laugh actually does — it comes after

mistake.display: saḥ parihāsam karoti, ca sā hasati.
mistake.why: ca has been put in front on the English pattern. It is postpositive: it follows the first word of the clause it joins, so the sentence needs sā ca hasati.

sentences.usage: The ordinary description of a joke landing, and the sentence a learner will want in the past tense within a day. Both halves matter — the laugh is the evidence the joke worked.

sentences.display: mama saṃskṛtam śrutvā aham eva hasāmi.
sentences.script: मम संस्कृतम् श्रुत्वा अहम् एव हसामि।
sentences.cue: Hearing my own Sanskrit, I am the one who laughs.
sentences.literal: my Sanskrit having-heard I indeed laugh

words.note: L1-M1's 'my'. It is what makes this a tease at the speaker and not at anybody else.
L1-M1's Sanskrit, as the object of the hearing. The ṃ inside it is internal and written in full — it is not a word-final nasal.
L4-M4's 'having heard'. It has no subject of its own: it borrows the main clause's, which is why the laugher and the hearer are the same person.
The subject of both halves — of the laughing and, through śrutvā, of the hearing.
L5-M1's emphasiser, lifting aham because it stands after it: 'I, of all people'. That lift is the whole joke.
The first-person shape of the laughing verb this module opened one sentence back. No separate word for 'am' is needed anywhere in the sentence.

sentences.trap: The gerund takes the main clause's subject and cannot have one of its own. So this can only mean that I heard and I laughed; to make somebody else laugh at my Sanskrit, the sentence has to be rebuilt.
sentences.sound: MA-ma sans-KRI-tam shroot-VAA a-HAM E-va ha-SAA-mi. śr is ś plus r, the ś being the sh of 'ship' said further forward. Said at speed saṃskṛtam śrutvā is saṃskṛtaṃ śrutvā, and śrutvā aham runs together into śrutvāham.

variations.changed: the subject changes and with it the gerund's owner, so this is no longer a self-tease — it is somebody laughing at me, which is a different sentence in every sense

variations.display: mama saṃskṛtam śrutvā aham na hasāmi.
variations.script: मम संस्कृतम् श्रुत्वा अहम् न हसामि।
variations.cue: Hearing my Sanskrit, I do not laugh.
variations.changed: negated; eva drops out with the laugh, because there is nothing left to lift

variations.display: mama saṃskṛtam śrutvā aham eva hasāmi, kintu saḥ na hasati.
variations.script: मम संस्कृतम् श्रुत्वा अहम् एव हसामि, किन्तु सः न हसति।
variations.cue: Hearing my Sanskrit, I am the one laughing — but he is not.
variations.changed: a second clause makes the contrast explicit, which is what the eva was pointing at all along

mistake.display: mama saṃskṛtam śrutvā eva aham hasāmi.
mistake.why: eva has slid in behind śrutvā, so it now lifts the hearing: 'merely on hearing my Sanskrit'. It lifts the word in front of it, and the word this sentence is about is aham.

sentences.usage: The one tease this register writes cleanly, because it needs no second person at all. It is also the safest thing to say in a room of better speakers, and it usually gets the laugh.
sentences.mnemonic: Aim it at yourself and the grammar stops fighting you.

sentences.cue: Sometimes a joke is not a good idea.

words.note: L3-M3's hedge. At the front of a sentence it reads as 'sometimes'; the same word inside a clause softens a claim to 'perhaps'.
The joke as the subject, so the plain shape. This is the sentence the module's second half turns on.
L1-M2's 'not'. With no verb to stand in front of, it negates the word that follows it — the adjective.
L2-M3's 'excellent', in its masculine shape because parihāsaḥ is masculine. An adjective agrees with the noun it describes and with nothing else.

sentences.trap: A verbless sentence still takes na. There is no 'is' for the na to sit in front of, so it goes in front of the adjective instead, and the sense is unchanged.
sentences.sound: ka-DAA-chit pa-ri-HAA-sah NA UT-ta-mah. The c of kadācit is the ch of 'church'. Said at speed parihāsaḥ na loses the visarga and runs on as parihāso na — the -aḥ turning into -o before the voiced n. The page keeps the -aḥ.

variations.cue: Sometimes a joke is a good idea.
variations.changed: the negation goes and the hedge stays, which is the other half of the same advice

variations.cue: Is a joke a good idea here?
variations.changed: the judgement becomes a question about this room, with L1-M7's atra doing the pointing

variations.display: kadācit parihāsaḥ na uttamaḥ, ataḥ aham na hasāmi.
variations.script: कदाचित् परिहासः न उत्तमः, अतः अहम् न हसामि।
variations.cue: Sometimes a joke is not a good idea, so I do not laugh.
variations.changed: L1-M9's ataḥ hangs a consequence off the judgement — and not laughing is a real answer to a joke that should not have been made

mistake.why: uttamam is the neuter shape and parihāsaḥ is masculine. An adjective takes the gender of its noun, so it is uttamaḥ here — the same agreement L2-M3 drew between uttamaḥ and uttamam.

sentences.usage: The module's 'when not to' in one line. Two cases in particular: a joke made in the classical register reads as mock-pompous, and a tease aimed at a stranger's bhavān reads as sarcasm because the politeness of the frame and the content disagree.
sentences.mnemonic: The joke agrees with nobody, but the adjective must.

words.note: L1-M1's 'this', agreeing with the neuter subhāṣitam.
L5-M1's subhāṣita, one rung back. A well-turned line quoted at the right moment is the wit this register carries most easily.
L4-M4's gerund, borrowing saḥ as its subject. He hears and he laughs, in that order and in one sentence.
The subject of both halves. It stands after the gerund here, which is the ordinary place for it.
The plain shape of the laughing verb, third person for one person. hasanti is the version for more than one.

sentences.trap: Nobody made a joke in this sentence. The laugh answers a SAYING — the pleasure of a line well placed — and that is a different kind of humour from the parihāsaḥ the rest of the module builds.
sentences.sound: i-DAM su-BHAA-shi-tam shroot-VAA SAH HA-sa-ti. ṣ in subhāṣitam is an s with the tongue curled back to the roof, quite distinct from the ś of śrutvā. Said at speed idam subhāṣitam is idaṃ subhāṣitaṃ, both m's softening to a hum.

variations.changed: the subject becomes a woman; a third-person present has no gender in it, so the verb does not move
the subject goes plural and the verb goes with it — hasati becomes hasanti, the same -anti L5-M1's vadanti showed

variations.display: idam subhāṣitam śrutvā saḥ na hasati.
variations.script: इदम् सुभाषितम् श्रुत्वा सः न हसति।
variations.cue: Hearing this saying, he does not laugh.
variations.changed: negated, which for a quoted line is a judgement on the room rather than on the line

mistake.why: hasanti is the shape for more than one person and saḥ is one. The verb has to match its subject in number, so it is hasati here.

sentences.usage: The wit of a well-turned saying, used for pleasure rather than for instruction. This is the humour a learner can reach at this level without any second person at all, and it is the one that travels.
sentences.mnemonic: The best joke here is somebody else's line.

sentences.display: aham parihāsam kṛtavān, kintu saḥ na hasati.
sentences.script: अहम् परिहासम् कृतवान्, किन्तु सः न हसति।
sentences.cue: I made a joke, but he is not laughing.
sentences.literal: I joke made, but he not laughs

words.note: The joker. The second clause has its own subject, so this one belongs to the first clause only.
The joke as the object of the making, one last time. This is the shape it takes whenever somebody makes one.
The participial past, agreeing with aham. The joke is finished; the trouble is in the present.
L1-M10's 'but', turning the sentence. Unlike ca, it does stand at the front of the clause it introduces.
The listener, reported in the third person. The whole difficulty of this module is that a listener addressed directly would be a bhavān, not a saḥ.
L1-M2's 'not', in front of the verb it negates.
Laughs — in the present, because the silence is happening now. This is the moment the retraction is for.

sentences.trap: kintu goes first and ca goes second. Two joiners, two positions, and this is the sentence to remember them by, because it needs one of each kind of turn.
sentences.sound: a-HAM pa-ri-HAA-sam KRI-ta-vaan, KIN-tu SAH NA HA-sa-ti. Said at speed aham parihāsam is ahaṃ parihāsaṃ, both m's softening to a hum. There is a real pause at the comma, which is where the joke has landed and not worked.

variations.display: aham parihāsam kṛtavatī, kintu saḥ na hasati.
variations.script: अहम् परिहासम् कृतवती, किन्तु सः न हसति।
variations.cue: I made a joke, but he is not laughing.
variations.changed: a woman says it, so the first participle forks and the second clause is untouched

variations.display: aham parihāsam kṛtavān, kintu saḥ na hasati, ataḥ kṣamyatām.
variations.script: अहम् परिहासम् कृतवान्, किन्तु सः न हसति, अतः क्षम्यताम्।
variations.cue: I made a joke, but he is not laughing — so, sorry.
variations.changed: the repair is bolted straight on with ataḥ, which is the whole module in one sentence: the joke, the silence, the withdrawal

variations.display: sā parihāsam kṛtavatī, kintu aham na hasāmi.
variations.script: सा परिहासम् कृतवती, किन्तु अहम् न हसामि।
variations.cue: She made a joke, but I am not laughing.
variations.changed: the two people swap places, so both the participle and the laughing verb move at once

mistake.display: aham parihāsam kṛtavān, kintu saḥ hasati na.
mistake.why: na has been put after the verb, on the English 'does not' pattern read backwards. It stands immediately in front of the verb it negates, so the clause is kintu saḥ na hasati.

sentences.usage: The honest end of the module. A tease with no retraction beside it has not taught the move, and this is the sentence that says why the retraction has to be ready before the joke is made.
sentences.mnemonic: Have the apology loaded before you fire the joke.

comprehensionPool.cue: Sorry — that was only a joke.

comprehensionPool.display: saḥ parihāsam kṛtavān, aham ca hasāmi.
comprehensionPool.script: सः परिहासम् कृतवान्, अहम् च हसामि।
comprehensionPool.cue: He made a joke and I am laughing.

comprehensionPool.display: adhyāpakaḥ parihāsam karoti, chātrāḥ ca hasanti.
comprehensionPool.script: अध्यापकः परिहासम् करोति, छात्राः च हसन्ति।
comprehensionPool.cue: The teacher makes a joke and the students laugh.

comprehensionPool.display: saḥ parihāsam kṛtavān, ataḥ aham hasāmi.
comprehensionPool.script: सः परिहासम् कृतवान्, अतः अहम् हसामि।
comprehensionPool.cue: He made a joke, so I am laughing.
